Descent

And there she was,

looking so pretty, shaded in a crevice between two buildings across the café. Her curly brown hair flowed past her shoulders, resting on a porous brown knit. As I approached, she flashed a brilliant toothy smile embraced by sun-kissed rosy cheeks, and at once I felt at ease…

Over coffee, she spoke of riots and protests in her home country. Of disillusionment with the world, and her plans to fix it. Of fantastic plans for flying machines and biomechanical fish. Of grandiose plots for world domination. In a moderately thick European accent she spoke, its origin I couldn’t place, but with each word she uttered I was drawn further in. There was something about her that was wildly charming. She fascinated me, like a puzzle I couldn’t quite figure out but had to solve. I wanted- No, I needed to know her…

We writhed and wriggled under bed sheets, her breath hot on my skin as she touched me. In the afterglow, our bodies entwined into a messy knot, and she whispered softly into my ear:

“Can I see you again?”

Crescendo

Click! She secures the collar around my neck, and I bite my lip. Ruby giggles.

“Oh, you like that, huh?” she croons.

I look into her eyes and nod silently. This taxi driver needs to hurry the fuck up. He doesn’t seem to understand the urgency of the situation he’s found himself in: two raging lesbians in his backseat are just a few minutes away from doing unspeakable acts to one another. Yet, he tools along like it isn’t Pride month, which it is. Asshole.

The cab’s interior is softly illuminated by intermittent streetlights, and is silent save for the soft hum of the engine and the pitter-patter of small raindrops on the windows. Ruby’s hand rests on my lower thigh, the half exposed by my miniskirt. I can sense her impatience rapidly building, and she looks at me with a mischievous glint in her eyes. Something stirs below: her hand disappears under my skirt, and she begins rubbing against me. I return the favor and feel her getting wet.

At last, the taxi stops and the car door swings open. Arigato-gozaimasu, the taxi driver croaks. Ruby fumbles with her wallet and practically throws money at the man, then shoves me through the door and onto the rainy street. She drags me to a nearby gray building, and pushes me against its wall.

Her tongue is down my throat, and we’re not even inside her apartment. It feels so good. God, I needed this. The two weeks since I last saw her have been near-incessant foreplay and yearning, but finally she is here with me, in the flesh.

She feels for her keys and clumsily swings her apartment door open while her other hand is up my skirt, and we collapse into a crumpled mess in the doorway. Slamming the door shut, she throws me against the wall, kisses down my neck, and sucks on my chest. Her arms slide down my waist and wrap around my thighs, lifting me off my feet and into her bedroom. I’m tossed onto her futon, my skirt and undergarments torn off, and flipped onto my stomach. Ruby presses herself into me.

Oh, fuck. I thought it would be good, maybe even very good, but not like this. I can…

barely…

even…

think anymore.

hrnnnnngggghhh

After what could have been five minutes or five days, there is a release of pressure and Ruby collapses beside me with a large sigh. I look down and see a viscous liquid stretching out from between my thighs, making a puddle on the sheets.

“Oh my god, baby,” I mutter while trying to catch my breath. “Fuck, I needed that so bad.”

She giggles, pulls me by my collar, and kisses me. “Good girl,” she purrs. “You took it so well.”

Epiphany

“See? Look around, we already live in a cyberpunk society,” Ruby says.

Great monoliths of concrete and glass tower above, while hordes of flesh push past one another on the cramped streets below. Steel death-boxes zip this way and that, screeching at any sorry flesh-beast that’s bold enough to cross their clearly delineated paths. The air is thick and smells of rot, coffee, fried foods, and sweat. In macro, it’s strangely beautiful, each individual a part of a greater organism. In micro, the grime and filth reveal itself: the mystery goo mashed into the pavement; crushed cans and plastic wrappers cowering in little corners and crevices; dried vomit from the night-before baking in the morning sun.

A woman with bright pink pigtails and ribbons in her hair, dressed in a tight crop top, barely-there skirt, and several inch-thick platform boots up to her mid-thighs; pushes through the crowd while tapping away on her personal communication slab. Click, clack! Her acrylic nails rapidly smack against the thing’s surface, while she chats aloud with some unseen interlocutor via plastic inserts in her ears.

I nod. “Cyberpunk, just without all the fun stuff that makes it maybe-kinda worth it, like cybernetic implants and hover cars,” I say.

“And half-naked, holographic girls dancing everywhere,” Ruby adds.

Just across the train station, we enter one of the gray monoliths and consult its directory, confirming the dermatologist’s office on the sixth floor. Proceeding into the structure’s guts, through a dizzying array of hallways we find the elevator hub. Within one of the lifts, an advertisement plays on the inside of its doors via a small projector mounted on the wall opposite. So cyberpunk.

“So stupid,” Ruby whispers in my ear.

The doors slide open and we bumble around the myriad offices in search of the dermatologist. It’s tucked in a dead-end, ominous and uninviting. Inside is a claustrophobic corridor-turned-waiting-room; at its far-end lies the front desk.

“Do you have an appointment?” the receptionist asks.

“No,” I reply.

“It might be a little while before we can see you.”

I turn to Ruby. “Are you sure you don’t mind waiting? You could go do something else, or I could come back another time.”

“Absolutely not,” Ruby says firmly. “We need to take care of you.”

I blush, and turn back to the receptionist. “That’s fine.”

She instructs me to fill out some intake forms by scanning a QR code with my phone. Ruby and I grab a couple of seats, and I begin inputting all of my information. Name, age, address, nationality… I smile to myself as I mark my gender as female.

The waiting room is baking, so Ruby leaves to find us some cold drinks. A few minutes later, I receive a message from her: a picture of her sticking her tongue out and exposing her breast. I hastily reply: do not get us kicked out lmao

After a wait that is long by Japanese standards but not so long by American standards, my name is called, and I enter one of the patient rooms. The doctor is already there. She asks where I’m from. I say America.

“So, English?” she asks in Japanese.

“Yes, or I can get by with Japanese,” I reply.

“Oh, okay.”

I tell her about my eczema flare-up, that I’m staying with my partner and using their products, so that’s likely the trigger. She agrees and writes a prescription.

A pharmacy is just down the hall, so Ruby and I waltz in and pick up my prescribed goods.

“Thank you for coming with me,” I say to her. “I know this probably wasn’t what you had in mind for our first weekend together.”

“Your health comes first,” she states matter-of-factly.

“Wow.”

“What is it?”

“No, I just-“ I start. “I’m not used to someone caring like this.”

She gives me a sad look. “Baby girl…”

We take the elevator down and emerge from the megastructure’s intestines. Ruby guides me down the street and through a train station toward her apartment. On the way, we cross a bridge with a tree at the end. Small, pale green fruit hangs from its limbs. Ruby stops and picks some, munching on one as she does.

“What is that?” I ask.

“I forget the name, but it’s safe to eat.” She tosses me one of the fruits. “Try one!”

I bite into it. Its skin is leathery and its flesh chewy, with a slightly floral, sweet taste. I shrug my shoulders. “It’s okay,” I say.

“What? They’re delicious!” Ruby fills a small plastic bag with about ten of the fruits.

I giggle. “I don’t know anyone else who would stop and pick fruits off a random tree on the street. You’re like a witch!”

“I’m gonna make a love potion,” Ruby says with wink.

We resume walking home. The buildings here are much shorter, only three stories tall at most, and the streets are far less busy. Here, the steel death-boxes are the main inhabitants. Sidewalks shrink and expand awkwardly, rudely interrupted by telephone poles and extruding buildings. This is a no man’s land; accommodation for creatures of flesh are an afterthought.

Ahead is a “My Basket,” a small neighborhood grocery store run by a large mega-corporation, with the corp’s logo shining in bright pink LED lights, so as to not-so-subtly remind that even small corner stores aren’t really local anymore. Crates of various vegetables line the front of the store, their prices printed in a faux-handwritten font.

“Let’s grab some bread for dinner,” Ruby says.

Inside, we pick up bananas for breakfast and bread for tonight. On the way to checkout, we scan through the ice cream selection, but nothing piques our interests. Instead, Ruby grabs a chocolate bar and says it’s for my train ride home tomorrow.

It’s extraordinarily mundane, yet weirdly romantic. I can see myself walking through the grocery aisles alongside Ruby years into the future. She’ll tell me about her day, I’ll tell her about mine, and none of it will be very interesting but that’s not the point. We’ll be happy to simply be in the presence of one another; to do life together. I really want this future.

I tug on Ruby’s arm. “Hey,” I say.

“Hi,” she says, smiling.

“I love you.”

Ruby makes a high-pitched squeal. “I love you, too!”

We embrace and share a long kiss. Then, we bring our bananas, bread, and chocolate to the checkout counter and walk the rest of the way home, her hand in mine.

Whiplash

“Oh my god, I’ve never cum from anal before,” Ruby says between heavy breaths. “Wow.”

I look to the bulbous toy in my hand, dripping with a clear substance, then to Ruby, now a crumpled mess on the futon. My lips curl into a smirk. I’m quite pleased with myself.

“Why don’t you go hop in the shower before dinner?” I suggest while massaging her back.

Ruby protests with an annoyed groan. “In a minute,” she mumbles. “Come here.”

I curl up beside her, claiming my place as little spoon. Ruby is always so warm and I’m always so cold, so we make excellent cuddle buddies. As her arms wrap around me, I immediately feel at peace. I could get used to this.

Eventually, Ruby loosens her hold on me. “Okay, I’m getting up,” she says sleepily and exits the room. A second later, her head pops around the door frame, like Kilroy.

“After my shower, I’m making you fried fish and okra!” she exclaims.

Her face disappears, and a couple of minutes later I hear the shower’s familiar hiss. I lay on the bed and stare at the ceiling, no doubt with a dumb smile plastered across my face. Fried fish and okra? I haven’t had it in years. Catfish and fried okra, the fish and chips of the South, are an old favorite of mine. Growing up, it was a staple comfort meal after church on Sundays. Two huge styrofoam boxes would be sat on the kitchen counter: one full of delicious, cornmeal-encrusted catfish (don’t forget the tartar); the other piled high with oily fried okra. I mentioned the dish to Ruby once before, but offhand. I never expected her to make it for me.

I’m not used to being romanced like this. This girl must really like me.

Ah, lesbians. Stereotyped for moving fast, and Ruby and I are no exception. Things have been progressing quickly between us. Really quickly. We’ve passed relationship milestones over the course of a couple of weeks that most couples don’t reach until months later. Despite all that, it’s felt natural. Right.

But also scary. I’m not ignorant of the myriad ways this could blow up in my face. What if I’m stepping into something I’m not ready for? What if Ruby isn’t who I think she is? What if I’m not who Ruby thinks I am? Everything feels so exciting right now, but when the novelty of it all starts to fade, will there be anything left? I think so, but I can’t be sure.

I met Ruby under the assumption of sex. We matched on a queer dating app one night and briefly exchanged messages. The following morning, we met at a café, chatted for about an hour, and went straight to my hotel afterward.

I expected her to see me as just a cut of meat: she would use me to get off, leave; I’d never hear from her again, and I’d feel shitty and embarrassed about the whole affair. Instead, she was a total sweetheart. She was patient and kind, constantly checking in with me, and asking for my consent. Her soft demeanor made me fall for her almost immediately. Ruby just felt safe—safer than anyone else in my life. It was easy to trust her.

If things go well between us, we can look back at our origin as a cute accident, an unlikely love story, evidence for “love at first sight.” But if things don’t go well, then it’ll be all too easy for someone to say, “Well, what did you expect?” And I wouldn’t have a good answer. To be moving this quickly—it is undeniably reckless.

But sometimes recklessness is exactly what is called for. After all, I found success in my transition by being reckless. I’ve refused to bend to anyone’s idea of who I am or what I should be, and I now reap the harvest of my efforts by living each day completely and fully as myself. To throw caution to the wind, to take a risk: sometimes rash decision-making lead to the best things in life. And maybe Ruby is one of those things.

Maybe.

My vision goes blurry and I feel my cheeks become moist. I hide myself under a blanket.

In January, my world flipped upside down after learning I was passing. In February, I realized that not only was I being perceived as a woman, but as an attractive woman, no less. A few months later, I have a gorgeous girlfriend and it’s getting very serious, very quickly. I’m getting everything I wanted, but on a timeline I never anticipated. It feels like my life is moving at light speed.

The hiss stops and Ruby walks past the doorway, humming a happy tune. I let out a sniffle a little too loudly, and she doubles back.

“Baby girl?” she says softly.

I grunt in a way to tell her I’m fine, which she ignores. Ruby lays down beside me and wraps her arms around me tightly. We stay like that for a while, saying nothing, just feeling each other’s warmth. It’s so nice.

After a time, she whispers into my ear, “Do you want to tell me what’s going on?”

I swallow. “It’s just a lot,” I manage.

“What is?”

“Everything. Us. It’s all happening so fast.”

“Yeah.”

“It’s a good thing! I’m happy. It’s just…”

“Overwhelming?”

“Yeah.”

Ruby squeezes me. “I understand, baby.”

I bury my face in her arm. “I know you’re about to start on dinner, but can we just lay here for a while longer?”

“Of course,” she says, and kisses my cheek.

In these arms, I could stay forever.

Sanctuary

“I’ll have an iced coffee,” I say to the barista.

They tap at a screen behind the counter. “That’s six fifty.”

Fishing through my purse, I produce a few coins and set them on a metal plate on the counter. The entry door chimes behind me, and I hear a familiar voice: Ruby.

I didn’t tell her I was coming today, so I decide to have a little fun. My outfit—a pink tube top, denim jacket, and a chiffon miniskirt—is brand new, so Ruby shouldn’t recognize me. She’s face blind. The only thing that could tip her off is my voice, so I remain quiet with my back to the door. This is a stealth operation.

The barista places my coffee on the counter, and I jam a straw between two ice cubes. Ruby chats idly with a couple others seated at the counter. I don’t know them. In fact, I don’t know anyone here except for Ruby. I’m a newcomer to this space.

I turn toward the sound of her voice, take a sip of my coffee—a bit watery for my taste—and stare at her. Ruby grows quiet and stares back at me with a confused look.

“Hey,” I say with a smile.

Her brow furrows. “Wait…”

She approaches me and scrutinizes my face. “What’s going on?” she asks. “Sage?”

I giggle. “It’s me!”

Ruby embraces me. “Why are you here?”

“I wanted to surprise you!” I exclaim, and reach for some flowers wrapped in parchment on the counter. “Here, these are for you.”

Ruby looks as if she’s about to cry. “No one’s ever given me flowers like this before.”

I frown. “I’ll make sure you get many more in the future.” I lean in and kiss her on the cheek.

“Wow,” Ruby says. “I can’t believe you’re here.” She stares at me and smiles, then grabs my hand. “Come on, let’s introduce you to everyone.”

We work our way around the narrow café: this is so-and-so, and they do such-and-such, and I met them at someplace, yadda yadda yadda. Each time we encounter a new face, Ruby introduces me as her girlfriend, and my heart skips a beat. Yes! Not only do I have a girlfriend, I am a girlfriend. Finally.

“Okay everyone, we’re going to start Ruby’s presentation,” a voice booms. “Find a cozy spot.”

Ruby plops herself at the back wall of the café, adjacent to a large projector screen displaying her presentation slides. Bold text reads: SMALL ACTS OF EVERYDAY RESISTANCE.

She gives some background on herself and her home country, then presents some alarming data about the rapidly deteriorating state of LGBTQ+ rights around the world, and offers some ideas on how we can fight back in small ways.

I haven’t seen this version of Ruby before, but I like her. She’s relaxed and well spoken; a natural presenter. It’s very attractive.

We break into small groups to discuss ways in which we can resist in our personal lives. I explain how I fought to use the women’s restroom at work. Someone else laments the callousness of their workplace’s leadership. Another discusses their trans partner’s difficulties living in Japan. A voice from across the room shouts, fuck AI!

I agree, disembodied voice. Fuck AI.

Eventually, Ruby’s presentation-turned-workshop ends, and the conversation drifts toward where to eat lunch. Ruby tugs on my arm.

“So, you’re staying the night with me, right?” she says emphatically.

“Um, well, is that okay?” I ask. “I don’t want to impose.”

“Absolutely! You must stay with me.”

I smile. “Okay,” I say and kiss her lips.

We bid the others goodbye, exit the café, and walk to the nearest train station. (Un)lucky for us, it’s the busiest train station in the world: Shinjuku Station, its labyrinthian halls infamously difficult to navigate. As we arrive at one of the behemoth’s entrances, Ruby turns to me with a pained expression on her face.

“I feel sick. Like, bad,” she moans.

“Do we need to find you a bathroom?” I question.

“I- I don’t know.”

She becomes unresponsive. I recognize what is happening: like me, Ruby is Autistic, and this is a classic example of a shutdown. No worries, I know what to do: take charge, give clear directions, ask yes or no questions, and get somewhere safe.

“Follow me,” I state.

Despite Shinjuku being a nightmare to navigate at times, I’ve been through the station enough times to know where I am. The closest restroom to us is near a shopping center. Taking Ruby’s hand, I push through the hordes and make a beeline for the restrooms, announcing each turn aloud in case we get separated.

Left. Right. Straight. Left. Left again. Straight. Up the stairs. Right. Here we are.

After some time, Ruby emerges from the restroom.

“Feel better?” I ask.

Ruby nods. “You were amazing!”

“What do you mean?”

“How you handled that. You took charge when I couldn’t make decisions. Thank you.”

I give a her a hug. “I can take care of you, too.”

Ruby smiles at me with stars in her eyes. I stare back. She’s so pretty.

“Come on,” I say. “Let’s go home.”

Submersion

Today is our first proper date, and we’ve already sort of botched it. We spent our entire morning sleeping, fucking, sleeping some more, and fucking again. By the time we stepped out of the house, it was hours later than we’d intended, and a torrential downpour had drifted in. Streets became rivers, and we had to shout just to hear one another over the storm. I asked Ruby if she wanted to turn around and spend the rest of the day inside, but she said no. She was determined to finally get out of the house and do something other than our usual routine of eat, sleep, fuck.

Also, Ruby was excited. She’d never been to an aquarium before, but she loves the ocean and everything in it. Aquariums are a rather cliché date spot in Japan, but it felt like a perfect choice for Ruby nonetheless.

And it seems I was right on the money. The moment we stepped into the place, Ruby’s eyes lit up. She looked at all the fish around us and gave me this look, like she wasn’t sure whether she wanted to press her face up against the glass or my lips. (She did both.)

Now, she’s enraptured by a tubular tank with silvery fish swimming in a circle, creating a mesmerizing display as the lights above reflect off their metallic scales. Ruby stares into the tank with a childish smile plastered across her face. She’s so cute. I tell her there’s a glass tunnel that runs through one of the tanks ahead, but I don’t think she hears me.

A child shrieks and breaks Ruby’s trance. “What?” she asks with wide eyes.

“There’s a glass tunnel ahead, where all the fish swim around you,” I repeat. “Look!” I point to an observation window, showing a large open fish tank below filled with all sorts of marine life and wavering silhouettes of people beneath the water’s surface.

Ruby looks she is going to explode with excitement. “Let’s go!” she screeches.

We descend a stairwell and emerge into the tunnel. A shark flys past us on our left side, an eel slithers past our right. The tunnel darkens as a massive manta ray soars above us, blocking the overhead lights.

Ruby is so absorbed, she doesn’t notice me admiring her, illuminated in pale blue as the surrounding water’s refractions dance across her face. She seems to get prettier each time I look at her, and in this light, she’s downright gorgeous.

Past jellyfish and crabs and lobsters and octopi, we end our time at the aquarium with the seal habitat. A round viewing platform looks down into the seal’s tank, with tall rocks jutting out from the water. One seal snores loudly on a rock, swaying back and forth with the waves. It looks like a gray oval with a face. Adorable.

The seal’s flipper slowly rises into the air, and quickly crashes down against its belly, making a loud smack! that reverberates off the enclosure’s walls. Ruby and I giggle for several minutes like schoolgirls, and my sides start to hurt.

These moments are a dime a dozen with Ruby. Each hour I spend with her is filled with laughter and smiles. Life is simply lovely with her.

We exit the aquarium, plunging into the wet onslaught once again, and I lead Ruby through the flooded streets in pursuit of dinner. Our destination: an upscale shabu-shabu—or hot pot—restaurant, its interior dark and moody with wood panel accents. Perfect for a date night.

We order the standard all-you-can-eat course, and engorge ourselves on pork and veggies, all the while talking about this and that. Our chatter is interrupted by occasional bouts of silence, as I stare into Ruby’s big brown eyes and she stares back into mine, and we stay like that for a while. These aren’t looks of mere admiration or lust. Ruby sees me in a way no one else does. She understands me: my convictions, my values, the way my brain works. With most people I feel like a mystery, but not with her.

Two hours later and a few pounds heavier, we brave the downpour once more and return home. We make love, then drift asleep in each other’s arms. In the morning, I awake enveloped in her warmth and it hits me:

I don’t have to be alone anymore.

Jubilee

I have come here to chew bubblegum and kick ass-

“…and I’m all out of bubblegum,” I quote along.

Screams echo through the bank’s marbled interior as a blonde mullet-ed man in sunglasses fires an impossible number of shotgun blasts into a panicked crowd while dramatic bass thumps along, like a heartbeat.

“Wait, this movie is where that quote is from?” Ruby asks, cackling.

John Carpenter’s They Live was a good choice. It’s the perfect mix of action, silliness, and anti-capitalist messaging that’s right up Ruby’s alley. The movies I’ve played for her in the past—like Clueless or The Devil Wears Prada—failed to hold her interest, but today she is glued to the screen.

Mr. Mullet is chased through the city by alien invaders, has a run-in with an attractive newscaster, and rallies his buddy to make a stand. The pair force their way to the news broadcast building and shoot their way to its rooftop. Then, a betrayal! The femme fatale has sided with the aliens, and kills Mullet’s partner. She shoots Mullet, too, and the camera zooms in on him as he bleeds out. He smiles, knowing his sacrifice isn’t in vain, as the broadcast’s antenna lies in pieces around him, interrupting the broadcast enslaving the human race. 80’s synth and electric guitar wails as credits swim up the screen. What a classic.

I close the laptop. “Do you want to open your birthday present?” I ask slyly.

“You got me a present?!” Ruby exclaims.

“Of course,” I say matter-of-factly. “I’m your girlfriend.”

I rummage through a closet, locate a bag concealed deep in its corner, then present it to Ruby.

“Happy birthday,” I chime.

Ruby has never really gotten anything for her birthday before, to the point where she preferred not to celebrate or acknowledge her birthday at all. I can relate. Growing up, my birthday was a reminder of all the things I tried so hard to forget: my lack of friends, the dysfunction of my family, another year passing while being no closer to feeling happy. As with Ruby, my birthdays became less about me and more about others: doing whatever was expected of me to just get through it. Birthdays became a chore; something to check off a to-do list each year. But no more. I was determined to break the cycle this year.

Ruby plunges her hand deep into the bag, spilling confetti on the floor. Inside is some jewelry, makeup, and an envelope. She carefully lays the contents out on a table, stares at it for a while, then looks at me with teary eyes. I give her a smile.

She slowly picks up the envelope and examines it closely. Its surface has her name in my handwriting, with a little heart. “No one has ever written me a letter before,” she says softly.

I give her a hug. I’m starting to get teary, too.

Ruby opens the envelope and reads the letter. It’s written using my usual formula: start off sarcastic and unserious to lower the stakes, then end with a strong emotional finish. It’s a home run. Ruby sets the letter down and her shoulders begin to tremble as tears rush down her cheeks. I wrap her up in a big hug and feel my shoulder become wet.

“It’s okay, baby,” I whisper softly. “We’re not going to have any more bad birthdays.”

She squeezes me tightly. “Thank you,” she mumbles, her voice hoarse.

After nearly an hour, Ruby collects herself. She lifts a pair of earrings off the table and smiles. “I love these,” she says, and inserts them into her ears. Two blue whales smile and dangle amidst her curls. She looks in the mirror at herself and beams.

“Let’s go on a walk,” Ruby decides. “There’s a nice park nearby.”

The outside air is hot against my skin, and so thick it feels less like walking and more like swimming. Not exactly ideal weather for a walk, but Ruby’s presence makes it just bearable enough. She leads me down the road to a set of a stairs built into a steep hill. At its top is a pleasant park encapsulated by bushy trees, its landscape dotted with fountains and benches. Children run this way and that, while bikers zip by on sidewalks, and a few scattered couples share private moments in the park’s shaded corners.

Ruby and I stroll over to a lookout point and gaze at the sprawling cityscape below, bathed in the golden light of the setting sun. I pull out my phone to take a selfie and Ruby rests her head on my shoulder, looking so tranquil. I don’t want this moment to end.

We stay there for a while, then make our descent from the opposite side of the hill and plunge into the city depths. The sun has just stooped below the horizon and the air is slightly cooler, although it’s still just as thick. Ruby leads me through several streets, then guides me into a fishing store hidden in a basement.

Fishing is one of Ruby’s hobbies and, naturally, one of her special interests. The moment we enter the shop’s threshold, Ruby ceases being my girlfriend and is immediately engrossed in the hundreds of fishing hooks, lures, poles, and various other doo-dads. I hover close to her, amused, until she lovingly tells me to go entertain myself elsewhere.

I was too distracting, I suppose. Hot girl problems.

Emerging from the shop’s depths, I locate a coffee shop, order a blended iced coffee, and plop down by a large window looking out at the street. The sun has fully set now, plunging the streets into darkness. The coffee shop’s bright interior reflects clearly on the glass, and a pretty girl stares back at me. She used to be a rare sight, but now I see her every day. So does everyone else. No one really sees a boy anymore. It’s nice.

I used to think of my current self and my pre-transition self as one and the same, but these days I see them more as separate entities. While my body has changed, so has my mind. I can’t see myself as a man any longer, even if I try. Likewise, I don’t think about being trans all the time as I once did, because it is an increasingly irrelevant detail in everyday life.

I’m just a girl.

I always assumed it would take years to reach passing status, if I ever did. But one year into my transition and I realized I was passing, forcing me to reckon with what was next. I came to understand that while the success of my transition felt good, it also felt hollow. I was lonelier than ever: isolated from most of my family, with a lack of friends, or anyone who understands what life is like as a trans woman. Essentially, my new body and mind didn’t mean anything without anyone to share it with.

Then I met Ruby and everything started to fall into place. Suddenly, all the pain and heartache I had undergone to realize my true self was worth it. Ruby understands me: the Autistic side of me, the trans side of me, and the uniquely Sage side of me. She’s my person. Life feels wondrous and exciting with her.

My phone rings: a FaceTime from Mom. I answer and tell her Ruby will join us soon. Mom is excited; it’ll be her first time meeting Ruby. Despite having only mentioned Ruby offhand to her a couple of times, Mom somehow recognized Ruby’s importance to me within our first month together. I was nervous she wouldn’t take us seriously given the relatively short amount of time we’ve been together, but she reassured me, saying, “When you know, you know.” Mother’s intuition, I suppose.

We chat about our week for a few minutes, and I spot Ruby enter the shop’s doors. She sits next to me, takes a sip of my coffee, and says hello to Mom. She shows us the things she bought at the store—hooks, lures, shiny things—and tells Mom about her birthday, flashing her whale earrings proudly.

The call goes well. Mom says Ruby and I are cute together before ending the call. I look over to Ruby, who is smiling at me. There’s so much love in that smile.

“Let’s get out here,” she says.

I take her hand, and she leads me from the coffee shop to the harbor nearby. A well-kept, urban park runs along the shoreline, and a few scattered couples have tucked themselves in little nooks. Ruby takes me to the harbor’s edge, right up to the railing, the sea waters quietly sloshing a few meters below. She takes my cheek in her hand, looks into my eyes, then pulls me close and kisses me.

We stay there by the railing for a while, holding each other close. Watching the harbor’s waves glimmer in the moonlight. Sharing silence. Enjoying the calm together. In this moment, I am completely at peace.

My head resting on her shoulder and her hand massaging my arm, I start to speak just as Ruby does the same.

In perfect unison: “I love you.”

Giggling, we begin walking back home, both of us relieved at finally having found someone to do life with.

Coda

Do you know why I love you?

It’s the way you delight in little critters.
It’s the way you melt when I say you’re pretty.
It’s the way you put me at ease no matter the situation.

Your eyes, big and brown, wondrously expressive.
Your hair, thick and curly, cheerfully bouncing as you step.
Your lips, pretty and soft, lovely when pressed against mine.

You bring out the best in me.
You help me be the woman I want to be,
and steer from the woman I was taught to be.

With you, I see a future big and bright.
One filled with smiles, laughter, and happy memories.
Hardships, too, but together we can overcome anything.

Strong, brave, intelligent, beautiful, kind —
You are all of these things and more.
I am so lucky to have met you.

For loving me,
for trusting me,
for sharing your light with the world —

I love you.

entry.title: about a girl
entry.content:
Photo by Oleg Ivanov on Unsplash

Somewhere
you’re out there.

Sipping coffee in a café
poring over a good book;
lounging at home on a lazy Sunday
buried under a mountain of blankets.

How’s the weather this time of year?

Are the trees in bloom
and the birds chirping their songs?
Or is everything slowing to a standstill
as Mother Nature settles in for her annual slumber?

I wonder
how do you wear your hair these days?

Do you let it down
or put it up in a ponytail?
Do you dye it bright colors
or let it glow in its natural beauty?

I think about you all the time:
how your hand fits perfectly in mine
how your laughter illuminates the room
how your warm embrace feels after a long day.

Tell me
do you feel it, too?

The yearning:
an endless void
an aching of the heart
a gaping cavity that can’t seem to be filled.

To desire
and to be desired—
this I crave more than anything.

I want you to love me.

Kiss me
caress me
stroke my hair
whisper into my ear.

Call me pretty.
Tell me everything will be okay.

I need you to fuck me.

Choke me
bend me over
spit in my mouth
make me your bitch.

Ravage me.
Make me cum.

Slowly suffocating
my hunger for you is a raging torrent.

I’m told it’s better this way
so I’m spared the heartbreak
but I don’t mind if you hurt me.

For if only a short time
it will have been worth it to have been loved by you.

entry.title: a warm winter’s night
entry.content:
Photo by Valentina Kondrasyuk on Unsplash

January. The harsh winter air spat at anything that dared step outside, as a cruel wind ripped and roared through the city streets. It was the sort of cold that seeped into one’s bones, chilling them from the inside-out. A bitter, violent cold.

That night, I barely noticed it, though. The frigid air parted in reverence as I walked along the river with her. Twinkling city lights danced across the water’s surface, making a dazzling display. Gorgeous, but it paled in the presence of her beauty. She led me to a spot overlooking a sleepy residential street, and we idly chatted by the riverside—the topic I cannot recall, only her brilliant smile and the melodic notes of her voice as she spoke softly to me. She rested her head on my shoulder and I felt like my heart might explode.

I should’ve kissed her then, but I didn’t.

She stayed close beside me as we strolled the mostly empty streets in search of a place for dinner. On her recommendation, we entered a small curry shop. A waitress guided us to our seats in the back, and we removed our coats, revealing what was underneath: me, in a simple white shirt and blue plaid skirt; her, in a long flowery dress. Our dishes were placed in front of us, but I hardly noticed. Normally, nothing can peel my attention away from a good curry, but in the presence of such beauty, how could I be bothered with such things? When she looked at me with those eyes, I was at once completely enraptured. Who wouldn’t be? She was just so pretty.

She invited herself over to my place, and I certainly wasn’t about to object. We laid on my bed beside one another—she lay no more than 20 centimeters away. I swear my skin was hot to the touch.

I wanted so badly to reach out and touch her, but I didn’t.

Our conversation stretched deep into the night. As the clock marched past its apex, I opened myself up to her, making myself wholly vulnerable against my better instincts. She responded with kindness and grace, and I felt understood in a way that I hadn’t experienced in years. My body was electric. It radiated so intensely, I could barely control myself.

Oh, but then that horrible moment! A lapse of judgement; a moment of insecurity; a severe miscalculation: I friend-zoned her.

It was an accident, of course. It sounds stupid, and I suppose it was. I couldn’t fathom that such a pretty girl could think that I, too, am pretty; let alone desire any form of intimacy with me! I wanted nothing more at that moment than to press myself against her, to show her how I felt about her, but I simply couldn’t reckon with the idea that such feelings could be reciprocated.

She left shortly after with a rushed, awkward goodbye. After the door clicked shut, I realized my mistake, but it was too late. She was already gone. I collapsed onto the floor and cried well into the morning.

As the sun peered over the mountains, I messaged her. We both apologized—what for, exactly, I’m not sure—but the damage was done. Things haven’t been the same since. Now we live our lives apart, devoid of one another’s warmth.

The nights feel much colder now.

entry.content:
Photo by charlesdeluvio on Unsplash

You called me pretty,
so I sent you pictures of my body.

Watching you get off to me,
makes me feel like the hottest bitch in the room.

It’s fun playing with you,
but it’s not enough.

I crave the real thing,
not a digitization via LCD.

I need a partner.

Someone to share
a laugh,
a cry,
a meal,
a weekend getaway,
(a bed),
in short—a life.

So I’ll keep making myself pretty,
in the hopes that one day I’ll meet her.

But until then,
I’d like to keep playing with you.

entry.content:
Photo by Krzysztof Kowalik on Unsplash

I heard you talking about me the other day.
You refused to call me your daughter,
Or even your son,
Just your “older one.”

I knew you wouldn’t accept me right away,
But I thought if I were open with you,
Maybe you’d come around.
Was I a fool?

We’ve grown so much closer over the past year,
Yet sometimes I feel farther apart than ever.
These words sit right below the surface,
Left unspoken so it stays comfortable.

This isn’t what I wanted for us.
I just wanted to be your daughter.
You know what I’ve endured to arrive here,
Still you act like I haven’t earned it.

I’m just a thing,
Something other than,
Something to talk around,
Never to wholly acknowledge.

Your love,
You claimed unconditional.
I told you I didn’t believe it,
And this is what I meant.

Your illusion of adoption;
My illusion of acceptance.
Your façade of empathy;
My façade of ignorance.

I don’t want to be less-than,
I’m tired of “coming soon.”
I desire nothing more than to just be,
Alongside you.

But maybe I’m wasting my time,
Hoping for a future that will never be.
Maybe I’ll never be anyone’s daughter,
Forever resigned to shattered memories.

entry.title: With you, I felt like a woman.

link.title: With you, I felt like a woman.

entry.content:
Photo by Janesca on Unsplash
📚 Table of Contents
  1. Thursday
  2. Monday, last week
  3. Saturday, last week
  4. Wednesday, last week
  5. Friday, last week
  6. Thursday, last week
  7. Monday
  8. Tuesday
  9. Thursday (and evermore)


Thursday

6 a.m. — Wake up, shower, throw on some makeup, pack up my things, and off to the airport. Try not to think about it.

11 a.m. — Board the airplane. I’m sandwiched between two strangers and I can’t stop crying. It’s awkward.

12:30 p.m. — Land at the airport. Pick up my suitcase from baggage claim and board a train to Tokyo. I’m seated next to Maddy and I’m crying. It’s awkward.

1:30 p.m. — Arrive at the station, give a rushed goodbye to Maddy and Luca, buy a shinkansen1 ticket, and head to the platform. I’m seated in-between a couple eating bento.2 I’m still crying. It’s awkward.

3 p.m. — Pull into my home station. Walk to a Starbucks and grab a hot chai latte, and head to the bus platform. A few other stragglers with suitcases board the bus with me. This time, I have a seat to myself, which is nice because I’m crying. But it’s still awkward.

4:30 p.m. — Reach the bus stop outside my apartment. Climb the steps to my door, roll my suitcase into the spare room, and collapse on my futon. I’m crying, but it’s not awkward anymore.

Buzz, buzz! It’s Maddy.

I think you look pretty when you’re crying

That’s something, at least.

Monday, last week

My phone vibrates. A message asks if I’ve packed yet. I reply: no lol

I leave for our trip in less than twelve hours, but no worries. I just have to throw some clothes in a suitcase. It shouldn’t take too long. What’s far more pressing right now, is that I need to make myself look like a girl as best I can. We need a girl shower, and we need to do some self-care. I pop my AirPods in and switch on my Bad Girl Club playlist. Let’s get to work.

Pluck eyebrows. Get bolder and pluck more than I’ve ever dared before, and hey, it looks good.

Squirt some shaving gel in hand, slather over legs, shave with razor. Do the same for my ass and chest. While I’m already in the area, boof the day’s progesterone. Then, epilator for the arms because it’s the only place I can stand the pain.

Finish with moisturizer and a face mask.

Tomorrow, I meet with Maddy and Luca, whom I haven’t seen in six years. Despite all three of us being genderqueer in some capacity, I still feel like I have to prove myself. I must be the best version of a girl that I can be. The last thing I want is to show up nearly a year into my transition, and have nothing to show for it. I have to be pretty.

It’s stupid and I know it, but I’m very insecure (and I know this, too). Maddy asked me the other day if I was excited about our trip. I gave her a mixed answer. I am excited to see them again after all these years, but I’m swimming in anxiety. The last two trips I’ve taken with friends in Japan resulted in those friendships ending immediately after, and those were before I transitioned. I don’t want that to happen again. Definitely not with these two.

So, if I can just be pretty enough; if I can just be friendly enough; if I can just be cute enough; if I can just be funny enough; if I can just be better, then maybe I’ll get through this trip with our friendships still intact.

My head hits the pillow a little after 1 a.m. Another buzz from my phone as our group chat is alight with excitement about tomorrow. I silence it. For now, rest. Tomorrow, it’s showtime.

Are you enjoying your first year?

No. It’s fucking hard and expensive and draining. It’s worth it, absolutely, and I’m really proud of the progress I’ve made. But I would’ve preferred to never have had to do this in the first place. Transitioning in front of everyone—my students, especially—is just embarrassing. Uncomfortable. All of this puts a certain degree of attention on me that I’ve worked my entire life to avoid. I don’t like the spotlight, but in order to move forward that’s where I have to be.

Saturday, last week

After deciding on what to order, I set the menu down on the dark wooden table. This TGI Friday’s is much cleaner than those I’ve encountered in America. The tables lack that dull sheen and stickiness so characteristic of many American chain restaurants, and the menu’s pages aren’t stuck to one another with some sort of mystery goo.

Maddy is seated next to me, with Luca across from them. Behind Luca, tall panoramic windows showcasing the Tokyo skyline stretch across the dining room, making him appear angelic as the blooming daylight casts him in silhouette and spills over its edges. Christmas music plays over speakers, and multicolored lights wrapped around the decor twinkle in sync. I sit there, enjoying the moment, knowing it’ll likely be one of the very few moments I have this year that actually feels like Christmas.

“Are we ready to order?” I ask, and everyone nods. I hail the waiter over. Maddy and Luca order cheeseburgers. I order mac n’ cheese, and onion rings for the table. The waiter departs.

We make some small talk as we wait for our food, but my friends are slaves to The Algorithm and inevitably their attentions turn to their timelines. I stare out the window and feel slightly smug at being able to stay off my phone for more than five minutes.

Luca looks up from The Algorithm and stares right at me. His brow furrows a bit. “For what it’s worth, I just forgot you’re trans,” he says, then turns back to his phone.

I don’t believe him. I believe he’s trying to be nice, but I don’t believe he earnestly forgot. Then again, that was a strange thing to say out-of-the-blue. Does he mean to imply that I pass? If so, he surely needs to get his eyes checked.

Still, no one has ever said such a thing to me before. I’m flustered and probably blushing. I’m not used to this sort of attention. Usually when I receive attention toward my trans-ness, it feels uncomfortable and invasive. But this? It feels good, even if he is just trying to be nice.

You know, I could get used to this.

Hey, do you find that your pants fit better since you started E? My pants are always falling down now. Like, look at this. My pussy is out!

Now that you mention it, I suppose so. I used to wear a belt every day, but now they’re more a fashion accessory than a necessity.

Wednesday, last week

Lock. The. Fuck. In. We’re an hour away from our Airbnb and our only hope of return is the last train of the night. We have to navigate these train stations and make these transfers flawlessly if we want to be sleeping in our beds tonight.

Normally, this would be no problem. I’m pretty good at navigating around Tokyo. The thing is, I’m absolutely plastered and I can’t walk straight to save my life. It turns out, estrogen has made me a bit of a lightweight! Oops.

We’ve got about a seven-minute walk from this izakaya3 to the station, a fifteen-minute train ride and a transfer after that, and a transfer after that. Also, I have to pee. Like, so bad.

Hold it in. There’s no time.

We make it to the station and step onto our train, and transfer to another train after. As I ride the train, my bladder screams at me. The absolute last thing I want to do is piss myself on the first day I see Maddy and Luca in six years. What would they think? Oh god, look at what E’s done to her. She’s a total mess!

Thankfully, our next train won’t depart for about ten minutes. Maddy needs to go, too, so I follow her to the restrooms. To the left is the men’s restroom, painted in blue hues. To the right is the women’s restroom, painted in pink hues. Maddy hugs a right immediately. I hesitate for a moment. Even in my sloshed state, I’m scared of following Maddy. Despite clearly presenting as a woman, I’m still hesitant to enter the women’s room. I have yet to make the switch. All it takes is one transphobe and my night’s over.

But honey, I ain’t using the men’s room in a fucking skirt.

Fuck it. I rush after Maddy and burst into a stall before my bladder does. Sweet relief. I exit the stall and wash my hands. My face looks blurry in the mirror. Strange, I didn’t expect to find the women’s restroom using funhouse mirrors. Then again, maybe it’s just the alcohol fucking with me.

It’s probably the alcohol.

Japan hates paper towels, so I shake my hands lightly to dry them. As I do, I look around and see:

A restroom. It’s not very interesting. It’s very normal, actually. It’s so normal that it’s incredibly mundane. I’m bored already.

And what’s this? That feeling of extreme discomfort of being the only one presenting as a woman in a room lined with urinals is… not here? Oh, huh.

And the transphobes, where are they? A trans girl is using the restroom and no one’s calling the police? Oh, huh.

You know, this is pretty alright.

Maddy smiles at me. “Ready?” she asks.

“Yeah, let’s go,” I stammer.

Does it shrink?

Yes. No. It’s a muscle, so it’s like a “use it or lose it” situation. It really sucked for a while after I started E because my sex drive was basically nonexistent, yet I still had to make things work. If you ever want bottom surgery, you still want all that tissue, you know? It’s better now since I’ve started progesterone, at least. It’s become a lot more enjoyable and doesn’t take me like two fucking hours.

Friday, last week

The map is an orgy of so many segments and floors, it’s difficult to make any sense of it. But one thing catches my eye: a Rainforest Cafe.

“Oh my god, they have a Rainforest Cafe!” I exclaim, bouncing on my toes. “I didn’t know these even existed in Japan!” Maddy and Luca don’t seem as enthused about this revelation as I am, but they’re amused by my excitement. “I loved these as a kid. Can we go, please?”

They agree, and we wander through the mall’s endless corridors for what feels like hours before we arrive at a familiar tropical scene. A small reception stand keeps watch before it, with a remarkably cute receptionist stood behind it. She has jet-black hair in pigtails, dramatic goth-lite makeup done, nose piercings, and a fashion sense that I can only hope to attain a small fraction of one day. Damn.

As the only Japanese speaker of our party, I step up to the stand and ask the girl if she could seat a party for three. She looks up at me with her dramatically styled eyes, and pauses for a brief second.

Anyone around me wouldn’t think twice of her reaction, but after living here for about four years, I’ve gotten pretty good at recognizing these brief little moments when someone is caught off-guard. I see it often whenever I visit anywhere that doesn’t see many foreigners: a split-second lowering of the socially mandated, outward-facing polite facade as the person thinks, Oh shit, a foreigner. What do I do?

These days, it’s more complicated. Now, it’s unclear whether the weird looks I receive are because I’m foreign, trans, or both. But seeing as we’re currently right outside of Tokyo Disney, the answer in this case is obvious.

The girl looks at me with confusion and a hint of disgust. It’s a look that reads: What are you?

I’ve received this look a lot today, and until this point I’ve been able to keep my cool. But receiving such a look from this girl at Rainforest Cafe feels like one too many. It feels like I’ve been reduced to a thing. Tears start to well up in the corners of my eyes, but I force them to retreat.

She tells me the restaurant is full. We go somewhere else.

Later that night, the three of us chat in the kitchen of our Airbnb. I excuse myself early, claiming I’m tired. Maddy and Luca chat for a couple more hours, while I wet my blankets with tears until I fall asleep.

Better luck tomorrow.

Are you going to stay in Japan for a while longer?

I guess. I don’t know what else to do. There’s not much waiting for me in America at this point, and that’s putting all the safety concerns with this administration aside. I’ve still got about a year-and-a-half left here, for sure. After, though? I dunno. Maybe I’ll stick around, or maybe I’ll go somewhere else. Thailand could be a decent option? I’d like to get bottom surgery one day. Maybe FFS,4 too, but I dunno about that one yet. How am I ever going to pay for any of that? No clue. But if I lived in Thailand for a bit, maybe I could get that stuff covered with insurance. That’s just an idea, though. I haven’t really looked into it. Thinking about what to do after all this is scary, so I try not to think about it most of the time.

Thursday, last week

My head is still pounding after overdoing it last night. I spent the morning and afternoon alternating between vomiting and sleeping, but I did my time and now I’m mostly okay. Maddy and Luca went out shopping, and I’m meeting with them in Akihabara because Luca wanted to visit it.

I haven’t been in years, but I’ve heard Akiba is a shadow of its former self. It’s true. Once the otaku5 mecca, now the place looks like something that once was, but no longer is. It feels sad. The fun hobbyist shops are mostly gone by now, and many of the arcades have gone to the wayside since COVID. It feels macabre, like a decaying carcass pawned off as a tourist trap. Many of the signs are English-forward, with speaker announcements barking advertisements exclusively in English, an occurrence I’ve barely encountered in my time living here. The only Japanese people in sight are the shop employees or the scantily clad maids lining the sidewalks in hopes to lure sad, horny men to their cafes. They must be freezing on this cool December night.

It’s still an enjoyable time among good friends, at least. We stroll down the main strip, idly chatting about little things we find along the way. Maddy spies an oven mitt with a Shiba Inu on it that they’re enamored with, and I buy it for her.

In time, we walk the length of the main Akiba stretch and decide to head home. The conversation has dried up, and we walk toward the station in silence, but it’s not uncomfortable. I think over the first couple of days of our trip thus far, then turn to Maddy.

“It’s strange,” I say. “You and Luca keep referring to me as ‘she’ and I find myself confused as to who you’re talking to.”

“Why? Aren’t those your pronouns?” they ask in a tone that implies I’m being ridiculous.

“Yeah, but no one really uses them. I mean, in Japanese there aren’t really gendered pronouns, so it doesn’t come up too much. I’m just not used to hearing people refer to me as a girl. It’s nice.”

“You are a girl.”

I smile. They’re right, of course. Of that, there’s no doubt, but I still haven’t grown accustomed to my gender being accepted and unquestioned. Everyone has heard about how difficult it is to get people to change how they refer to and see you, but many people don’t realize how difficult that can be for yourself, too. Transphobes might claim this is proof that one is just deluding themselves, but it’s only natural for it to take time to get used to seeing yourself in an entirely different light than what you’re used to.

These days, I look in the mirror and am frequently taken aback—Who’s that girl? Wait, that’s me. It’s not that I don’t believe I’m a girl, but the image I have of myself in my mind seems to lag behind reality. It’s similar to when I adopted my chosen name. At first, it felt strange being referred to by a name different from the one I’d been called for the first two decades of my life. It felt good, but it took some time for my brain to adapt to “Sage = me.”

It’s the same with pronouns. Maddy and Luca haven’t slipped once, though. We’ve spent a good chunk of time together, too. I’m starting to believe that perhaps they’re not simply entertaining me—maybe they genuinely see me as a girl.

And you know what? I’m starting to genuinely see myself as one, too.

I’m so glad you’re finally happy.

Hmm. “Happy” is relative and often feels like it’s not for people like me. But, I’m getting there.

Monday

This conversation is boring me to death. For the past hour, it’s been nonstop K-pop idol gossip and talk about pop culture that soars right over my head. I’ve never felt older.

The alcohol isn’t doing its job. Typically, when I feel awkward and out of place, it’s a great option to quell the anxiety that eats away at my insides. But tonight, this beer just isn’t cutting it. I’m stone-cold sober and, oh god, here we go again about some rapper I’ve never heard of…

At least this place is cute. A bizarrely labyrinthian, pastel-colored, two-story okonomiyaki6 joint in the heart of Dotonbori run by a bubbly Japanese woman. The walls are plastered with little signs in flowery handwriting explaining all manner of things. There’s more text on the walls than paint, yet I’m running out of things to read. I try to look entertained. We’re meeting with Grace tonight, who we haven’t seen in six years, and I don’t want to make a bad impression.

Now they’re talking about someone called Sexyy Red. Who are these people? And when did I become so out of touch?

I excuse myself to the restroom. It’s tucked away in a brightly colored corner, and it’s horribly claustrophobic, as restrooms in Japan often are. I have to press myself up against the wall to make enough space to even open the door. I shut it behind me, and let out a long sigh. A bored-looking girl stares back at me in the mirror. I practice some expressions to feign amusement, but give up. I’ve never been good at hiding my boredom.

Squeezing myself back through the doorway, I return to my seat. My beer glass is empty. Luca is saying something about Tennessee. He’s very drunk, and his words are heavily slurred. A white woman from the table next to us looks up, seemingly annoyed, and corrects Luca on the population of Tennessee. She says she knows many things about the populations of American states. Luca asks what the population of Nashville is. She says Nashville isn’t a state. I stifle a laugh. The woman rolls her eyes and returns to her food. The conversation turns back toward people I’ve never heard of.

With nothing to contribute to the current act of socialization taking place before me, I try to convince myself I’m not actually there. I’m unsuccessful, though. My mind basks in anxiety. While everyone at our table is queer, I’m the only clocky trans person present. Luca transitioned years ago and just looks like a normal dude, while Maddy and Grace present conventionally female. I stand out like a sore thumb, in my purple cardigan and long black skirt, with my face that’s somewhere between boy and girl. To a random passerby, I may as well have a sign above my head that reads QUEER ALERT!

At last, our party decides to move on from this place. Good timing, too—I was just starting to get overstimulated by all its bright colors and echo-filled chambers. We shuffle out onto the dark Osaka streets in search of an arcade, and I hang a few paces back from the group. I consider making up some bullshit excuse to turn in early, but I decide against it. It’s Luca’s birthday and I don’t want to ruin it.

As we near Namba Station, Luca realizes I’m sulking. He turns to me, a little wobbly on his feet, and places one hand on each of my shoulders—perhaps to steady himself, but I’ll give him the benefit of the doubt. Looking me right in the eye, he says, “Look, I wouldn’t normally say this, but I’m kinda drunk right now and…” His words are horribly slurred, and normally I would feel quite uncomfortable to be so close to a man—drunk or sober—yet I feel perfectly at ease in this moment. There’s an earnestness in his voice. It’s endearing.

“Sage, you’re beautiful! You’re absolutely gorgeous!” he says a little too loudly. “Like, you look soooooo good. You’re still in your first year of transition, and you look that good already? It’s craaaaazy.” My heart skips a beat, maybe two. It’s like he was reading my mind and knew just what to say. Maybe I’m not as good at hiding my emotions as I thought.

“That’s really sweet,” I reply, “but I’m clocky and I know it. I don’t pass. On the plane this morning, a stewardess came up to me and said, ‘Sir, please put your bag below the seat in front of you.’ Like, I’m wearing a skirt, a full face of makeup, nails done, and I’m still getting misgendered.”

Luca waves his hands in drunken dismissal. “I still had people that would call me a girl for a while. Even when I grew out my beard, they’d decide my voice was too high, and suddenly I’m a girl to them. But, you look good, girl.”

This is the most emotion I’ve seen from Luca throughout this whole trip. He’s laying it on a little thick, but it’s kinda cute.

Maddy and Grace join in, agreeing with Luca. “You look really pretty, girl,” they say. “Seriously.”

I blush and look away. I’m not used to all this praise.

“I try really hard. Even still, my voice sounds like a man,” I protest. “And fair enough, I haven’t done any voice training yet, but-”

Luca’s face scrunches up. “No,” he says. “No! Your voice is totally androgynous.”

Maddy and Grace nod in agreement. Of this, I know they’re lying. I’ve heard recordings of my voice. They’re just being nice. Regardless, it’s really sweet.

Luca continues showering me with praise. He goes on and on about how pretty I am, how I should feel good about myself, and how well I’m transitioning. Truthfully, it feels a bit like pandering, but I appreciate it nonetheless.

Maybe they’re right. Even if I don’t pass, so what? Who’s to say “pretty” is limited to only those strictly adhering to gender norms, which are bullshit anyway?

I may still have a long way to go, but that doesn’t mean I can’t be pretty now.

I walk a little taller. I sway my hips a little more. I let my wrists loosen, and sink into this warm feeling. I’m a woman. Fully. Not sorta-a-woman, not half-a-woman, just a woman. Just another girl on the street.

I smile and walk to the arcade with everyone, no longer lagging behind.

I’m working two jobs. Sometimes I go into work around 2 a.m., sleep during the day, and head to my other job in the evening. Just trying to make rent! At least I’m not working at Amazon anymore.

I can’t imagine. I dunno how you do it—I’d be dead after the first week, if that. Though, I can’t say I’m faring too much better, financially. It feels like I’m just scraping by since starting my transition, and I don’t really have a plan to change that. That’s the thing, isn’t it? People like us—we don’t tend to care much about things other people do, like a career. We don’t have that luxury, you know? I’ve got this friend; she’s got all these plans for the future. She’ll talk about how this and that is going to lead into these other things. She talks about things like savings. She talks about eventually settling down one day, maybe. I can’t relate. I’m out here just trying to survive. Every day is a battle. I’m just happy to still be here. But, I’m living paycheck-to-paycheck, you know? Like, how am I supposed to plan for the future when I can’t predict tomorrow? I turned 28 last week. For most of my life, I didn’t think I’d even be alive at this age. I’m making it up as I go.

Tuesday

As we approach the mass of people, I spot Luca and Grace near the back. I give them a wave and push through the crowd toward them, with Maddy following close behind. Everyone’s eyes are fixated on a stage where men are dancing with what looks like evil Hello Kitty as it sings a song. It sounds truly awful to my ears, but the crowd seems to be into it.

I look to Luca. He appears to be enjoying himself, but he never looks unhappy. Grace is enthralled with the performance, occasionally miming dance moves along with the performers. Maddy gives me a look that says she’s feeling the same way I am and mouths, I need to pee.

I nod. “Me too,” I say. “Let’s go.”

We break out of the crowd in search of a restroom. We’re in the Hollywood area of Universal Studios Japan, made to look like an idyllic early 20th century America. The sun has set, and the streets are illuminated by cast iron streetlights. It’s almost magical.

Ahead of us is a restaurant styled like an old diner, complete with checked floors and cherry red booth seating inside; smooth curves and a chrome finish outside. “I love the look of old-fashioned diners,” I say.

“I was just thinking that!” Maddy exclaims.

“Honestly, I just really love that early 20th century American aesthetic. It’s so expressive.”

“I love the fashion.”

“Oh my god, yes! Like those flared dresses in bright colors?”

“So cute. You should wear one!”

“Ah, I don’t have that kind of confidence.”

“Well, I didn’t mean right now.”

We find a restroom tucked behind the diner. My skirt’s zipper gets stuck, and I fumble around with it for a few minutes. After I finish, Maddy is already waiting outside for me.

“So, um,” I start, “do you like, want to go back to whatever that was?”

They laugh. “Not really.”

“Thank god. It was so loud. Let’s go find somewhere to chill.”

After a bit of aimless wandering, we take a seat on a bench set against a small lake. It’s peaceful. The park’s lights bounce off the water, creating a van Gogh-esque scene in the reflection. The Flying Dinosaur, a Jurassic Park themed roller coaster, extends over the water. Every minute or two, a car zooms past on its rails, with distant screams reverberating in its wake.

“There’s still an hour-and-a-half left until the park closes,” I state.

“Anything else you want to do?” Maddy asks.

I check the park’s wait times on my phone. JAWS has a 30-minute queue.

“Well, there’s JAWS. The wait isn’t bad!”

“Ooh, JAWS sounds fun. Want to go?”

“I mean, they’re still watching that show, though. Do we just go without them?”

Maddy shrugs. “We could.”

“I don’t want to make them mad, though.”

“We don’t have to tell them.”

“Ha, that seems like a bad idea.”

Luca and Grace approach from behind and sit next to us. Grace tells us about another show she wants to go to. It starts in 30 minutes. I groan, but not loudly enough for anyone to hear.

Grace looks at Maddy and me. “We should go early so we can get a good spot,” she says. “Let’s head over, unless, like, you guys want to sit here some more.” Luca and Grace depart.

“Did you hear that?” I ask Maddy.

“Hear what?”

“Grace. She was like, ‘Let’s go, unless you wanna sit here some more,’” I say in a mocking voice. “Like, okay bitch! I just wanted to sit and rest my feet for a bit, damn.”

Maddy laughs. “I guess we should go,” she says.

“Yeah,” I reluctantly agree.

The show is a musical about a group of friends gathering for Christmas. Inexplicably, the show is 90% Japanese and 10% English, with no translations of any kind on offer. Yet, the characters apparently understand each other perfectly. It’s also woefully over-acted in typical Japanese fashion, which I’ve always found grating. I pull out my phone and message Maddy, to keep my bitching private.

we could be on jaws rn

I know
This blows

lmaooo

Sworry
Ten minutes in and I was like damn I’m ready for it to be done

it’s really 30min

Yeah
Fuck

Eventually, the show ends and we exit the park. Grace takes the lead and begins hunting for a place for dinner.

Luca and Grace chat while they look for a restaurant, while Maddy and I follow loosely behind. Maddy points out a guy she thinks is cute.

“Yeah, he is cute,” I say, my voice starting to trail off.

“You good?” Maddy asks.

“Yeah, sorry. I was just thinking about something else.”

“About what?”

“Oh, um,” I pause. “Don’t worry about it.”

“Ah, come on!”

“Fine. I was thinking about how bad I want a girl to rail me right now.”

“Oh?” Maddy giggles. “Like who?”

“I don’t think I care too much right now.” I snap out of it. “Sorry, I started progesterone last month, and it’s really kickstarted my sex drive. It’s kinda driving me crazy.”

Maddy begins to say something, but Grace shouts over her shoulder, “How about Hard Rock Cafe?”

It seems our unofficial directive for this trip is to hit up as many American chain restaurants as we can find. I don’t miss America much, but sometimes I get an itch that nothing can scratch quite like multi-thousand calorie, overpriced mediocre food served on gigantic plates. Hard Rock Cafe sounds perfect.

“Sure,” I say.

Maddy looks at me and whispers, “We’ll finish this conversation later.”

We’re sat at a window-side table by one of the most attractive women I think I’ve ever seen. As she explains the daily specials, I pinch myself. Is this real right now?

After she leaves, Maddy says the waitress is really pretty. Grace and Luca agree.

“Oh my god, right?” I say, trying to keep my voice at an even tone. “She’s gorgeous.”

“You should tell her that,” Maddy says.

“Yeah, put yourself out there,” Grace agrees.

“Absolutely not.” I shake my head. “There is no way in hell I’m saying anything to her.”

Grace and Maddy exchange a look of mild disappointment.

“Ooh, the bartender’s super cute, too,” Grace chimes.

I whip around in my seat and the table erupts in laughter.

“You turned so fast!” Grace bellows. “I’ve never seen you move so quickly!”

I giggle. “He’s pretty cute, but nothing like our waitress.”

The table fills with laughter once more.

God, this is so nice. Chatting shit, talking about cute boys and girls, idly bitching—I feel like one of the girls. No, I am one of the girls. It’s all I ever wanted. This is why I transitioned. This makes all the pain worth it.

Could’ve gone to JAWS.

We should totally be on JAWS right now.

Thursday (and evermore)

I’ve cried a lot over the past year, but today just might take the cake. I’m impressed there’s still enough moisture left in my body for tears. My eyes feel like leaky faucets, and I can’t turn the knobs hard enough to shut them off.

Strange as it may sound, I like crying. For many years, I was completely unable to cry, which denied me the cathartic emotional release it provides. As an emotional person, this was hell.

But today, I’ve cried for about twelve hours straight. I’m over it. I would like to stop, but I don’t seem able to. The truth is, I’m in mourning.

Of course, I’m going to miss being around Maddy and Luca. The past week-and-a-half has been so much fun, and we all still like each other now that it’s over. We’ve made many great memories that I’m sure we’ll continue talking about years into the future. But we’ve also spent 99% of the time we’ve known each other apart. I’ll be fine.

It’s more than that. Maddy and Luca saw me as a girl, without exception. They used my pronouns without error. They didn’t deadname me once. They told me I look pretty. They treated me like a girl, and scoffed at any notion of doing otherwise. I wasn’t less-than, I was.

It was the first time I’ve experienced such treatment since I started transitioning. With them, I didn’t have anything to prove. I was a girl whether I had my makeup done or not; whether I was presenting overtly femme or not—no matter what.

But now it’s over. I have the weekend to myself, but come Monday I must return to my usual day-to-day: an uncomfortable place of occasional deadnaming and misgendering, confusion around bathroom use, and the constant disconcerting feeling that I have to prove myself. That I have to be better. That I have to be more woman than any other woman around me because all eyes are on me.

It’s back to the daily hum-drum of: what are you?

I’m no longer a woman. I’m a trans woman, at best. These tears are to lament the loss of my brief womanhood.

As I lay there on my futon, my hair spilled across my dampened pillow, I recall an exchange with my mother:

i just hate that me just existing creates these awkward situations for you. it’s not fair to you at all, you didn’t ask for this
i mean i didn’t either i guess, but you know

You existing does not create awkward situations. Other people’s inability to see that your decisions aren’t about them is what makes awkward situations.

thanks mom, i needed that. love you

I love you, too! Don’t let anyone make you feel bad about who you are. You are amazing and courageous and I am honored to be your mom!

The tears fall at a waning pace now. My mind drifts to Michelle, and the little I Saw the TV Glow keychains she made for my birthday.

My thoughts were if you’re ever having a rough day you can look at them and remember where you started and how far you’ve come, and that you’re more strong and capable than you may think or feel in that moment.

Transition is fucking hard. It’s one of the hardest things a person can do. Over the past year, I’ve spent an incredible amount of time, effort, and money to get where I am now. I’m broke and I’m tired and I’ve undergone so much pain to get here, too—both mental and physical. Hours of agonizing at my face in the mirror. Hours of plucking hairs and blasting my skin with lasers. Was it worth it?

Abso-fucking-lutely.

In January, I took a selfie the day I started HRT. I looked upon that picture and felt hopeless. There was no way a girl could ever be made of that! My skin was rough and ugly, and my hair was thinning at a concerningly rapid rate. I looked old and tired. But a year later, my skin looks supple and young, and my hair has filled in. I feel great.

In June, I had the crash-out of the century. I bitched about shaving and always cutting up my face—I no longer have this problem. I bitched about my bulge not allowing me to wear the pants I wanted—I no longer have this problem. I bitched about eyeliner being impossible to apply—I no longer have this problem. I bitched about never wearing a dress or a skirt—I wear skirts all the time now. I bitched about never being able to afford laser for my face—I’m five sessions in now. I bitched about not seeing a girl in the mirror—I see her all the time now.

In July, I wrote about feeling so hopelessly ugly. Now, I no longer have to tell myself I look pretty in the hopes that one day I’ll believe it. If I start to doubt myself, all I need to do is to peer into the mirror and the doubt fades away. Once, mirrors were the most terrifying things on the planet. Now, I find them affirming. A year in, I never expected to be where I am now. If this is where I’m able to reach after just a year, I can’t wait to see where I am at the two, three, four, five year marks. Luca was right. I’m transitioning beautifully.

Something happened at the eleventh month. It was as if everything started to click into place, and I could clearly see the fruits of all my efforts finally coming to fruition. While I still haven’t reached my final destination, I am proud of who I am in the current moment, and Maddy and Luca taught me that I’m not crazy for feeling that way. They brought out a self-confidence in myself that I haven’t felt in years.

I’m a girl, and I don’t care what anyone says, I look good.

The tears cease at last, and I drift into a peaceful rest. I don’t know it yet, but the coming weeks will bring about the most difficult challenge yet in my transition. But this time, I will be ready. This time, I know who I am and that I’m worth fighting for.

Transition is hard, and filled with countless hurdles that try to snuff you out. But I’m stronger.
